title: Approach to blistering diseases
summary: Sort a blistering rash by where the skin splits (subcorneal, intraepidermal, subepidermal), whether it is immunobullous, and how fast to refer. Biopsy for immunofluorescence is done by specialists, but the referral speed is decided in primary care.

glance.think: Blisters or erosions without an obvious burn, bite, friction or infection.
glance.engine: Autoantibodies against desmosomes (intraepidermal, flaccid) or hemidesmosomes (subepidermal, tense); drugs; infection; genetics (EB).
glance.backbone: Identify the pattern, refer at the right speed, look for a drug cause, and prescribe and monitor within the specialist plan.
glance.never_miss: SJS/TEN, pemphigus with mouth erosions, eye involvement, pemphigoid in pregnancy, eczema herpeticum and SSSS in children.

what: A **vesicle** is a fluid-filled lesion under 5 mm (some texts say 10 mm) and a **bulla** is a larger one. An **erosion** is loss of epidermis only, often all that remains of a fragile, superficial blister. The depth of the split explains what you see. The higher the split, the more flaccid the blister and the more erosions there are. The deeper the split, the more tense the blister, and haemorrhage, scarring and milia can follow.

list: **Flaccid blisters or erosions only, with oral ulcers** suggest pemphigus (PV), or SJS/TEN if acute and the patient is unwell.
**Tense blisters, sometimes haemorrhagic, on an urticarial or eczematous base in an elderly person with itch** suggest BP.
**Excoriations and tiny grouped vesicles on extensors and buttocks, intensely itchy** suggest DH.
**Fragile blisters, scars and milia on the backs of the hands with hypertrichosis** suggest PCT (or pseudoporphyria, or EBA).
**A "string of pearls" annular arrangement** suggests linear IgA disease (often drug-induced, e.g. vancomycin).
**Flexural erosions with fissured maceration** suggest Hailey-Hailey. **Sudden, painful, targetoid or dusky skin with mucosal involvement** suggests SJS/TEN.

features: The **Nikolsky sign** (shearing the epidermis off with lateral pressure) is positive in PV, SSSS and TEN, and *usually* negative in BP. The **Asboe-Hansen sign** (pressure spreads the blister edge sideways) points to PV.

diagnosis.h: (specialist workup that the IP should know)

list: **Two biopsies** (this is the tutor's summary point): **Lesional**, from the edge of a **fresh** (<48 h) blister, for H&E (split level, acantholysis, eosinophils/neutrophils), sent in formalin; **Perilesional**, from normal-looking skin about 1 cm from a blister (or uninvolved skin for DH), for **direct immunofluorescence (DIF)**. Send it in **Michel's medium** or fresh on saline gauze, **never formalin**. Biopsy of an eroded or ulcerated site gives a false negative

**DIF patterns** (use photos A06 and C05): intercellular **"chicken-wire/fishnet" IgG ± C3** = pemphigus; **linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ** = BP/MMP/PG; linear **IgA** = LAD; **granular IgA** in the dermal papillae = DH; perivascular IgG/C3 and "doughnut" deposits = PCT
**Salt-split skin** separates BP (epidermal roof) from EBA (dermal floor).

**Serology:** ELISA for anti-Dsg1/Dsg3 (titres roughly follow activity) and anti-BP180/BP230; indirect IMF; for DH, **tTG-IgA + total IgA** (± EMA); for paraneoplastic pemphigus, anti-envoplakin/periplakin

**Baseline for systemic therapy** (the IP will be asked about these): FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose/HbA1c, BP, weight, bone profile + vitamin D, **TPMT** (azathioprine), **G6PD** (dapsone), hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV serology, TB screen (IGRA/chest X-ray) before rituximab or high-dose steroids, a pregnancy test, and immunoglobulins before rituximab.

**Do not start oral steroids "to see" before biopsy unless the specialist advises it.** They reduce the diagnostic yield, and in DH/coeliac a gluten-free diet would do the same to serology.

Supportive care while waiting for an urgent appointment: bland emollients and a soap substitute; puncture large tense blisters at the base with a sterile needle but leave the roof on; non-adherent dressings (silicone/paraffin gauze) and no adhesive tape on fragile skin; a potent or superpotent TCS **only** for suspected BP once dermatology agrees; analgesia, plus benzydamine/chlorhexidine mouthwash or an antiseptic mouthwash for oral erosions

**Medication review is the IP's core skill:** gliptins, loop diuretics, spironolactone, PD-1 inhibitors, thiol drugs (penicillamine, captopril), vancomycin, NSAIDs, and recent new drugs (SJS/TEN window 4–28 days).

red_flags.h: Blistering red flags and referral routes

head: Presentation
Why it matters
Route / timeframe
rows: Widespread painful skin, dusky/target lesions, **detachment**, **≥2 mucosal sites**, fever; new drug in the last 4–28 days
**999 / ED now.** Stop culprit drugs. Ask ED to involve on-call dermatology and ophthalmology; burns or ITU transfer
Widespread erosions **± oral ulcers**, unable to eat or drink, dehydrated or hypotensive (Case 1)
Fever, unwell, **facial oedema**, widespread rash, eosinophilia, abnormal LFT/U&E, 2–8 weeks after a new drug
Pustular sheets on erythema with fever 1–2 days after an antibiotic
Same-day dermatology advice; admit if unwell
Child, febrile, tender red skin with superficial peeling, mucosa spared
Eczema with sudden clustered punched-out erosions, fever, unwell
Same-day: start oral aciclovir if well; if unwell, eye involvement or infant → admit (see the [eczema](condition:eczema-dermatitis) notes)
Eye pain, red eye, photophobia, reduced vision, or symblepharon with blistering
Hoarseness, dysphagia or stridor with mucosal blistering
Pregnant woman with periumbilical urticated plaques and blisters
Elderly person with new tense blisters, not systemically unwell
**Urgent dermatology** (within ~1–2 weeks; teledermatology photos speed triage). Medication review now
Persistent oral erosions (>3 weeks) ± skin erosions
Urgent dermatology or oral medicine. **Suspected-cancer (2WW) pathway** if a single non-healing ulcer
Grouped itchy excoriations on extensors ± gut symptoms
Routine dermatology + gastroenterology; coeliac serology **on gluten** first
Same-day assessment; low threshold to admit

red_flags: **IP do's:** stop suspected drugs; document; take photos; give fluid, analgesia and dressing advice; check for steroid or immunosuppressant use; Yellow Card.

**IP don'ts:** don't start oral prednisolone for undiagnosed blistering without a specialist discussion; don't put adhesive dressings on fragile skin; don't de-roof tense blisters; don't advise a gluten-free diet before coeliac tests.
pearls: Ask about **mouth, eyes and genitals** at every blistering consultation. Mucosal involvement changes the urgency and the referral route.
Infection risk: crusting, pain, fever or a sudden spread of erosions may mean secondary *S. aureus* or HSV. Swab and treat.

head: Post
Statement
Correction
rows: EB occurs at **three** levels. **EB simplex** is intraepidermal (basal keratinocyte, keratin 5/14). **Junctional EB** is in the lamina lucida (laminin-332, collagen XVII). Only **dystrophic EB** (collagen VII) is dermolytic, below the lamina densa. EBA (acquired, collagen VII) is also dermolytic. See the [infant skin pages](condition:neonatal-rashes) notes

Furosemide is a fair example, and etanercept is a case-report association. **Add DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins), the best-established and most relevant to primary care**, plus spironolactone and PD-1 inhibitors
Correct. SSSS also belongs here (exfoliative toxin cleaving Dsg1, the same target as PF).
Pemphigus = vulgaris, foliaceus, erythematosus, vegetans, paraneoplastic
Good. Add **IgA pemphigus** and **drug-induced** pemphigus. Erythematosus is a localised form of PF, and vegetans is a variant of PV
That is PV or DH. BP is **subepidermal with linear BMZ IgG/C3**
"DPP-4 inhibitors are a common cause of drug-induced bullous **pemphigus**; lisinopril can prevent it"
Gliptins cause **pemphigoid**. ACE inhibitors (including lisinopril) are a *weak cause* of pemphigus, not prevention. There is no evidence that lisinopril prevents gliptin-associated BP
IVIG works by blocking CD95 (Fas) in TEN
That was the in-vitro rationale. Clinical evidence is mixed, and the UK 2016 guideline does not routinely recommend IVIG. Ciclosporin is often preferred
